extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in political economy and institutional design
extracted.subtask_description: Normative and diagnostic criteria about when joint-stock companies and public educational institutions are appropriate, how they should be funded and governed, and what practices promote or undermine teacher diligence and useful curricula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of a trade for joint-stock management (reducible to routine)
rubrics_metrics.description: The only trades fit for joint-stock management without exclusive privilege are those whose operations can be reduced to a routine or to such a uniformity of method as admits of little or no variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: banking; insurance (fire, sea risk, capture); making/maintaining a navigable cut or canal; bringing water to a great city. Rationale: routine operations allow management by directors who cannot be expected to maintain unremitting individual vigilance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly/exclusive privilege often required for joint-stock foreign trade
rubrics_metrics.description: Without a monopoly a joint-stock company cannot long carry on any branch of foreign trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: many competitors in both buying and selling markets require unremitting vigilance and dexterity that company directors usually fail to provide; monopoly cushions companies from the discipline of competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater and general utility as justification for joint-stock establishment
rubrics_metrics.description: To render a joint-stock establishment reasonable it ought to appear with the clearest evidence that the undertaking is of greater and more general utility than the greater part of common trades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility must be substantial compared to ordinary trades; mere capacity to manage something successfully is insufficient justification for special corporate privileges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of capital size for joint-stock establishment
rubrics_metrics.description: A second requisite is that the undertaking requires a greater capital than can easily be collected into a private copartnery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a moderate capital suffices, private adventurers would supply demand and there is no need for a joint-stock with special privileges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating exemptions for private advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unreasonable to establish a joint-stock company merely because it might manage an undertaking successfully or to exempt a particular set of dealers from general laws simply because they might thrive with such an exemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public policy should not grant special corporate exemptions for narrow private benefit; such exemptions distort competition and social welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical caution: frequent failure/mismanagement of joint-stock companies
rubrics_metrics.description: Many joint-stock companies established for foreign trade have failed from mismanagement, notwithstanding exclusive privileges; joint-stock companies often support negligence, profusion, and malversation of their servants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical evidence of failures to temper enthusiasm for corporate forms; do not assume extraordinary profits or superior management solely from corporate structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banking is particularly suited to joint-stock form
rubrics_metrics.description: The principles of banking practice are capable of being reduced to strict rules; joint-stock companies are often more tenacious of established rules than private copartneries, making them well fitted for banking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Banks require large capital supporting public credit and occasional advances to government, which private copartneries may not muster; note legal peculiarities (e.g., Bank of England's limitation on number of persons in other banking companies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insurance trade suitability criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of risks (fire, sea loss, capture) admits of gross estimation and is reducible to rule and method, so insurance may be carried on successfully by a joint-stock company without exclusive privilege.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: London Assurance and Royal Exchange Assurance had no exclusive privilege. Manageability of risk estimation supports joint-stock organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infrastructure (canals, aqueducts, water supply) suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: When a navigable cut or canal has been made, management becomes simple and reducible to strict rule; such undertakings often require large expense and are therefore suitable for joint-stock companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction can be contracted at fixed rates per mile/lock; long-term operation is routine and fits corporate management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding source for educational institutions (avoid burdening general revenue)
rubrics_metrics.description: The expense of institutions for the education of youth need not be charged upon the general revenue; endowments commonly arise from local/provincial revenue, rents of landed estates, or funds placed under trustees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public endowments often do not require central government funding and historically have been financed by local or private sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of endowments on teacher incentives (diminished necessity of application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Endowments and salaries independent of performance diminish the necessity of application in teachers; where emoluments are independent of success and reputation, teachers have weaker motives to exert themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When pay does not depend on results, teachers may neglect laborious duties or perform them carelessly; competition and the need to earn subsistence promote exertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee-based remuneration preserves some incentive
rubrics_metrics.description: In some universities the salary is but part of a teacher's emoluments; the greater part arises from fees of pupils, and reputation and dependence on students preserves incentive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where student fees form a significant portion of income, teachers remain motivated to deserve favourable sentiment and maintain diligence to attract pupils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of fees (salary-only) sets interest against duty
rubrics_metrics.description: If the teacher is prohibited from receiving fees and his salary constitutes his whole revenue, his interest is set in direct opposition to his duty and he is likely to neglect it or perform it slovenly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This funding structure creates perverse incentives: with identical pay regardless of effort, the rational choice is minimal effort unless externally compelled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal collegiate governance encourages mutual indulgence
rubrics_metrics.description: If authority rests in the body corporate of the college (composed of teachers) they are likely to make a common cause and be indulgent to one another, consenting that neighbours may neglect duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-governance by peers can blunt accountability and reduce overall teaching quality; examples: many Oxford public professors long ceased to teach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problems with extraneous jurisdiction and oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Extraneous jurisdiction (bishop, governor, minister) can force attendance on lectures but cannot dictate their quality; oversight by persons ignorant of the subject is arbitrary and degrading for the teacher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External enforcement tends to be limited to quantitative measures (number of lectures) and may encourage obsequiousness to protect office rather than genuine diligence or improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student allocation and privileges affect emulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Forcing students to certain colleges (through privileges of graduates or apprenticeship-like statutes) makes them attend independently of teacher merit and tends to extinguish emulation among colleges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies that reduce student mobility or attach students to institutions by non-meritocratic means weaken competitive pressures that encourage teaching quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charitable foundations and attachment of scholars reduce choice and emulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholarships, exhibitions, bursaries that attach students to particular colleges independently of merit diminish emulation; prohibiting students from leaving without leave extinguishes competitive improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing scholars freedom to choose institutions could increase emulation and incentives for colleges to improve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tutor appointment without student choice reduces diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: If tutors are appointed by heads and students cannot change them when negligent or unable, emulation among tutors is extinguished and overall diligence diminishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Student ability to choose or replace tutors promotes accountability; denying this option encourages complacency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad teaching methods as a marker of poor institutional incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers may read a book in a dead language to students, have students interpret, or occasionally remark — a sham lecture that discipline forces attendance upon; this manifests low effort rewarded by institutional structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: reliance on ceremony and discipline to feign teaching. Genuine, well-prepared lectures remove need for coercion and attract students voluntarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good lectures remove need for coercion after early youth
rubrics_metrics.description: After twelve or thirteen years of age, provided the master does his duty, force or restraint can scarcely ever be necessary to carry on education; no discipline is requisite to force attendance upon lectures which are really worth attending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in lecture quality and relevance rather than coercive discipline; students are generous and forgiving to teachers who show serious intent to be useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private instruction often superior for practical skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts of education with no public institutions (fencing, dancing, reading, writing, accounting) are generally best taught privately and seldom fail of being learned when privately taught.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical/vocational skills may be better delivered by private instructors subject to direct fees and competition rather than by public institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curricular choices should be guided by the ends of the institution and practical utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally universities focused on theology and languages useful to churchmen; study of subjects (Greek, Hebrew) was introduced as need arose for original texts and practical ends (e.g., reformation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curricula ought to reflect the actual purposes (professional or civic) for which institutions exist; inclusion of subjects should depend on demonstrable utility for those ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize logic and experimental sciences over metaphysical subtleties
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic (science of good and bad reasoning) should be taught prior to other sciences; historical university emphasis on metaphysics/pneumatics over experiment led to neglect of experimental natural philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training students to distinguish probable from demonstrative arguments and to reason well is foundational. Educational systems that overvalue metaphysical subtleties at the expense of observation and experiment hinder practical knowledge.
